notes:
Task and constraints: Compute maximum binary-tree width at any level, counting missing positions between the outermost non-null nodes.
Idea: `widthOfBinaryTree` performs level-order traversal with conceptual indices, computes `q[-1][1]-base+1`, and renormalizes child indices by subtracting the first index.
Technique and why it applies: Complete-tree positional indices preserve gaps between sparse nodes; level-local normalization limits index growth without changing widths.
Invariant: `q` contains one level in left-to-right order, and each index represents that node's position among all conceptual positions at that level.
Edge cases: A null root returns zero; a single-node tree has width one; sparse branches retain gap positions through their indices.
Complexity: Each node enters and leaves the queue once, giving O(n) time and O(n) worst-case queue space.
complexity_reason: The stored positional indices preserve gaps, while subtracting the first index keeps each level's numbers small.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest level width including null-position gaps between the leftmost and rightmost real nodes.
Idea: `widthOfBinaryTree` maintains parallel `nodes` and `idx` lists, computes width from the first and last indices, and assigns children indices `2*i` and `2*i+1` after normalization.
Technique and why it applies: Conceptual complete-tree indices encode absent positions; using `long` avoids overflow during index arithmetic for wide levels.
Invariant: Each pair in the lists identifies a node and its left-to-right position within the current level.
Edge cases: Null root returns zero; a leaf yields width one; gaps are counted even when intermediate child positions are absent.
Complexity: Each node is processed once for O(n) time, and level lists use O(n) space; the result is cast to `int` per the method signature.
complexity_reason: Long indices represent conceptual positions, and level normalization preserves width while reducing numeric growth.

notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether at most one element can be modified so `nums` becomes non-decreasing; this implementation mutates the input list.
Idea: `checkPossibility` counts adjacent inversions and, at the first one, lowers the previous value when `i < 2` or `nums[i] >= nums[i-2]`; otherwise it raises the current value.
Technique and why it applies: Choosing which side of the inversion to adjust preserves the earlier prefix whenever possible and avoids spending more than one modification.
Invariant: After handling an inversion, the processed prefix is non-decreasing if a valid single change remains possible.
Edge cases: Empty and one-element arrays return true; a second inversion returns false immediately; input values may be changed in place.
Complexity: A single left-to-right scan gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The comparison with the element two positions back determines whether lowering the previous item preserves order.

notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether an integer array can be made non-decreasing by changing at most one element; the method modifies the array directly.
Idea: `checkPossibility` counts each `nums[i] < nums[i-1]` inversion, rejects a second one, and selects which endpoint to adjust using `nums[i-2]`.
Technique and why it applies: Lowering the previous value is safe when it does not violate the earlier prefix; otherwise raising the current value is the feasible local choice.
Invariant: Once an inversion is repaired, the prefix through index `i` remains non-decreasing under the chosen single modification.
Edge cases: Arrays of length zero or one return true; a second descent returns false; callers should expect possible mutation.
Complexity: The loop runs once over the array, yielding O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The `i-2` comparison selects the repair that keeps the already processed prefix valid.

notes:
Task and constraints: Construct a permutation of values 1 through `n` with exactly `k` distinct adjacent absolute differences.
Idea: `constructArray` alternates the low endpoint `lo` and high endpoint `hi` of the range 1 through `k+1`, then appends the increasing suffix from `k+2` to `n`.
Technique and why it applies: Alternating endpoints produces successive large and small differences, covering the required `k` distinct differences; the suffix adds only difference one.
Invariant: After each loop iteration, `out` contains a permutation of the consumed endpoint values and realizes the intended descending set of differences.
Edge cases: For `k=1`, the alternating section is `1,2`; when `k=n-1`, no suffix remains; valid constraints require `1 <= k < n`.
Complexity: Every value is appended once, so time is O(n) and output space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Alternating the range endpoints creates the distinct differences before the consecutive suffix adds only ones.

notes:
Task and constraints: Build an array containing each integer from 1 to `n` once with exactly `k` distinct adjacent absolute differences.
Idea: `constructArray` writes alternating `lo` and `hi` values through `k+1`, then fills the remaining slots with consecutive values beginning at `k+2`.
Technique and why it applies: Endpoint alternation creates the `k` distinct difference values, while the increasing tail contributes only difference one.
Invariant: `i` is the next output slot, and each iteration consumes the smallest and largest remaining values in the alternating prefix.
Edge cases: The valid problem constraints require `1 <= k < n`; if the alternating endpoints meet, the inner conditional prevents an extra write; `k=n-1` yields no tail.
Complexity: Each output position is written once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space for the result array.
complexity_reason: The conditional after writing `lo` prevents overwriting a slot when only one endpoint remains.

notes:
Task and constraints: Trim a BST so every retained node lies in inclusive range `[low, high]`, preserving BST ordering.
Idea: `trimBST` discards a node below `low` by continuing into its right subtree, discards one above `high` by continuing left, and recursively rewires children for an in-range node.
Technique and why it applies: BST ordering proves that when a root is too small its left subtree is also too small, and when too large its right subtree is too large.
Invariant: Every returned subtree contains only in-range values and retains the BST property.
Edge cases: A null root returns null; values exactly equal to either bound remain; recursion depth can reach tree height.
Complexity: Each visited node is examined at most once, giving O(n) time and O(h) recursion space.
complexity_reason: BST ordering lets the algorithm skip an entire out-of-range side instead of visiting every node.

notes:
Task and constraints: Remove BST nodes outside inclusive bounds `low` and `high` while preserving the order of all retained nodes.
Idea: `trimBST` recurses right when `root.val < low`, left when `root.val > high`, and otherwise replaces both child links with trimmed results.
Technique and why it applies: The BST invariant makes the opposite subtree irrelevant when a root falls outside one bound, so whole regions can be skipped.
Invariant: Every returned node and descendant has a value in range, with valid BST links maintained.
Edge cases: Null returns null; boundary values are kept; an unbalanced tree may cause recursion depth O(n).
Complexity: Each visited node is handled once for O(n) time, with O(h) stack space where `h` is tree height.
complexity_reason: The root comparisons safely bypass the subtree that cannot contain any in-range values.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest distinct value greater than the root value in the special tree, or `-1` if none exists.
Idea: `findSecondMinimumValue` sets `first` to `root.val`, traverses with `dfs`, and updates `second` for values above `first`; such nodes stop recursion because descendants cannot improve the candidate under the special-tree property.
Technique and why it applies: In this tree each parent is the smaller child value, so once a node exceeds the root minimum, its descendants cannot contain a smaller second-minimum candidate.
Invariant: `second` is the smallest qualifying value encountered so far, with infinity representing absence.
Edge cases: Null root returns `-1`; duplicate root-minimum values are traversed; if no greater value exists, infinity maps to `-1`.
Complexity: Each relevant node is visited at most once, giving O(n) time and O(h) recursion space.
complexity_reason: The special parent-minimum property justifies pruning below a node already greater than the root.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the second distinct minimum in a special binary tree, returning `-1` if no value exceeds the root minimum.
Idea: `findSecondMinimumValue` initializes `best[0]` to `Long.MAX_VALUE` and calls `dfs`; `dfs` updates it for a value above `first` and prunes that node's descendants.
Technique and why it applies: The special tree guarantees parent values are the smaller child values, so descendants of a node greater than the root cannot improve the candidate.
Invariant: `best[0]` is the smallest qualifying value visited; the sentinel indicates that no qualifying value has appeared.
Edge cases: Null root returns `-1`; repeated values equal to `first` trigger further traversal; `long` sentinel avoids collision with ordinary integer node values.
Complexity: The traversal takes O(n) time and O(h) recursion space for tree height.
complexity_reason: The long sentinel distinguishes the absence of a candidate from any valid integer node value.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest contiguous strictly increasing run in `nums`.
Idea: `findLengthOfLCIS` handles an empty list, then increments `cur` only when `nums[i] > nums[i-1]`, resetting it to one otherwise and tracking `best`.
Technique and why it applies: A single pass suffices because each run can be summarized by its current length and the longest length seen.
Invariant: At each index, `cur` is the strictly increasing contiguous suffix ending there, and `best` is the maximum run length seen so far.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; equal adjacent values break a strictly increasing run; a single element returns one.
Complexity: Each element is compared once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Resetting on equality or descent ensures only contiguous strictly increasing segments contribute to the maximum.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the longest length of a contiguous strictly increasing subsequence in `nums`.
Idea: `findLengthOfLCIS` returns zero for an empty array and updates `cur` using `nums[i] > nums[i-1]`, then updates `best`.
Technique and why it applies: The optimal run ending at each position depends only on the previous adjacent comparison, so dynamic programming needs just two counters.
Invariant: `cur` measures the increasing run ending at the current index; `best` is the best run found anywhere in the scanned prefix.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return zero; equal neighbors restart the run at one; singleton arrays return one.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The algorithm needs only the previous element and two counters, avoiding a separate DP array.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether `s` can be a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
Idea: `validPalindrome` moves inward while endpoints match; at the first mismatch it tests `pal(l+1,r)` or `pal(l,r-1)`.
Technique and why it applies: Any valid one-character deletion at the first mismatch must remove one of those two endpoints, so testing both remaining ranges is sufficient.
Invariant: Before the first mismatch, all compared endpoint pairs match; each helper call checks whether one allowed deletion leaves a palindrome.
Edge cases: Empty and single-character strings return true; an already-palindromic string needs no deletion; only one mismatch may be bypassed.
Complexity: The outer scan and at most two helper scans cover O(n) characters total, so time is O(n) and auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Only the two mismatching endpoints can be deleted to repair the first unequal pair.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return whether a string becomes palindromic after zero or one character deletion.
Idea: `validPalindrome` scans inward and on the first unequal pair tests `pal(s,l+1,r)` and `pal(s,l,r-1)`.
Technique and why it applies: A single deletion must remove either character at the first mismatch; the helper verifies each candidate remainder without constructing a new string.
Invariant: All endpoint pairs before the first mismatch are equal, and `pal` checks every pair in the selected remaining interval.
Edge cases: Empty strings and already-palindromic strings return true; both candidate ranges may be tested; no more than one deletion is permitted.
Complexity: The initial scan plus at most two linear helper scans is O(n) time, with O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The helper validates an index interval directly, avoiding allocation of candidate substrings.

notes:
Task and constraints: Evaluate score operations: numeric values add a score, `C` removes the previous score, `D` doubles it, and `+` sums the previous two.
Idea: `calPoints` keeps valid scores in `scores`, applies each operation using the last one or two entries, then sums the remaining list.
Technique and why it applies: A stack-like list represents the current valid scoring history, so cancellation removes the last entry and derived scores can access recent entries directly.
Invariant: After each operation, `scores` contains exactly the valid score history produced by all operations processed so far.
Edge cases: The input is assumed valid, so `C`, `D`, and `+` always have enough prior scores; an empty operation list returns zero.
Complexity: Each operation performs O(1) amortized list work and final summation is O(n), giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The list retains only active scores, making cancellation and recent-score operations constant time under valid inputs.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the final baseball score from integer operations and `C`, `D`, and `+` history operations.
Idea: `calPoints` processes each string in a switch, mutating list `s`, then iterates over the valid scores to compute `sum`.
Technique and why it applies: The list stores the active score history; each operation can cancel, double, or combine the most recent values according to the rules.
Invariant: After each operation, `s` represents all currently valid round scores in order.
Edge cases: Valid input is assumed to provide enough scores before `C`, `D`, or `+`; no operations returns zero.
Complexity: Processing and final summation take O(n) time, while the score list stores up to O(n) entries.
complexity_reason: Each operation touches only the tail of the score history, followed by one final linear sum.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the extra undirected edge that creates a cycle in a graph formed from a tree plus one edge.
Idea: `findRedundantConnection` initializes `parent` and `rank`, finds each endpoint's representative with path compression, and returns the first edge whose endpoints already share a representative.
Technique and why it applies: Union-find maintains connected components; an edge within one component closes a cycle, while union by rank keeps trees shallow.
Invariant: Before processing each edge, DSU components match connectivity induced by previously accepted edges.
Edge cases: A valid problem input guarantees a redundant edge; the fallback returns an empty list if none is found; labels are assumed within the initialized range.
Complexity: With path compression and union by rank, operations take O(α(n)) amortized and total time is O(n α(n)); arrays use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The same representative means a prior path already connects the endpoints, so the current edge closes a cycle.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the redundant edge that first creates a cycle in an undirected tree with one added edge.
Idea: `findRedundantConnection` initializes `p` and `rank`, calls path-compressing `find`, and unions representatives unless they are already equal.
Technique and why it applies: Disjoint-set union tracks components incrementally; equal representatives prove the edge connects vertices already connected by earlier edges.
Invariant: After every successful union, each DSU set represents one connected component of the processed graph.
Edge cases: The valid input includes one redundant edge; `find` compresses paths recursively; the returned array is the original edge reference.
Complexity: Union by rank plus path compression gives O(n α(n)) total time for `n` edges and O(n) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Path compression and rank balancing make representative queries nearly constant amortized time.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum number of edges in any path whose nodes all share one value.
Idea: `dfs` obtains child path lengths, extends `a` or `b` only when that child matches `n.val`, updates `self.best` with `a+b`, and returns the larger one.
Technique and why it applies: A path through a node may combine matching arms from both children, but a parent can extend only one arm upward.
Invariant: `dfs(n)` returns the longest same-value downward path in edges starting at `n`, while `self.best` records the global path maximum.
Edge cases: Null nodes return zero; leaves contribute zero edges; if child values differ from the parent, their arms contribute zero.
Complexity: Each node is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(h) recursion space.
complexity_reason: The helper returns one extendable arm while the global answer can combine both matching arms.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest path, measured in edges, where every node has the same value.
Idea: `dfs` computes child lengths, extends `a` and `b` for matching child values, updates field `best` with `a+b`, and returns `max(a,b)`.
Technique and why it applies: Combining both compatible child arms gives the best path through the current node, while returning only one arm allows its parent to extend a valid path.
Invariant: `dfs(n)` returns the longest downward same-value path from `n`; `best` stores the maximum path found anywhere.
Edge cases: Null returns zero; a leaf's path length is zero edges; a mismatched child contributes no extension.
Complexity: One postorder visit per node yields O(n) time and O(h) call-stack space.
complexity_reason: The postorder result supports parent extension, and the field records paths that bend through any node.
